Idiopathic Toe Walking
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Walking on the toes or forefoot without heel strike on initiation of the stance phase of gait
Can occur normally as a child develops the gait pattern; toe walking beyond age 2 years
requires investigation to rule out neuromuscular or developmental abnormalities1 (Resource
1).
Epidemiology
Prevalence of 2% to 5% at age 5.5 years in the general population
Prevalence of 41% in children with neuropsychiatric diagnoses or developmental delay
Etiology
Unknown

Etiology
The etiology is largely unknown; however, proposed causes include defects in sensory
processing, abnormalities of underlying muscle fibers, and a possible genetic
component. In 10% to 88% of patients, a family history of toe walking is noted, and
autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete expression is suspected.
Natural History
A study revealed a 5% prevalence of toe walking in patients aged 5.5 years. In more than 85%
of these patients, the condition resolved without management by age 10 years.

Natural History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062

A Swedish study followed 1,401 healthy children without known motor or neurologic
developmental conditions. The overall prevalence of toe walkers at age 5.5 years was 5%
(63 children). By age 10 years, only 8 of the 63 children who were originally toe walkers
were still toe walking2 (Resource 2).
Classification
Alvarez classification3 (Table 1)
Type 1: short triceps surae with heart-shaped calf (Figure 1)
Type 2: positive family history and V-shaped Achilles tendon (Figure 2)
Type 3: periodic tiptoe walking that resolves spontaneously

Figure 2 Photograph of an ankle shows a V-shape on the Achilles tendon, which is observed with
the foot dorsiflexed. (Reproduced with permission from Pomarino D, Ramírez Llamas J, Martin S,
Pomarino A: Literature review of idiopathic toe walking: Etiology, prevalence, classification, and
treatment. Foot Ankle Spec 2017;10[4]:337-342.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Overview
A thorough patient history and physical examination should be performed to rule out
neurologic and developmental causes of toe walking.

Overview
Patients may or may not be able to walk flatfooted, depending on the degree of equinus
contracture. If limited ankle dorsiflexion is present, surgeons must determine whether
contracture is caused by the gastrocnemius alone or the entire gastrocnemius-soleus
complex. Persistent limitation of dorsiflexion with knee extension and flexion is
secondary to contracture of the gastrocnemius-soleus complex, whereas equinus that
improves with knee flexion indicates gastrocnemius contracture.
Patient History
May provide a history of poor balance, frequent falls, pain, fatigue, ankle sprains, or muscle
cramps

Patient History
Caregivers generally notice idiopathic toe walking at toddler age if the patient has a gait
abnormality compared with his or her peers. The patient may have issues with calluses
or stress fractures or difficulty with shoe wear. The primary concern may be cosmetic,
social, or pain related.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
5/32

Physical Examination
Full lower extremity physical examination, including assessing femoral and tibial version,
ligamentous examination, neurologic examination, and the Gower test.

Physical Examination
Attempt to observe patients from afar before they are aware they are being watched.
Assess gait from the front, side, and back, and assess hip, knee, and ankle motion during
gait. Assess neutral standing position, evaluate leg lengths, and assess for muscle
atrophy. Evaluate the range of motion of the hips, knees, ankles, and subtalar joints.
Assess callosities on the plantar aspect of the forefoot and/or absence of thickened
glabrous skin along the plantar heel. Finally, surgeons must perform a Silfverskiöld test.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs of the foot and ankle are indicated in patients with rigid equinus deformity.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Brain and spine MRI for abnormal neurologic examination
Other Studies
Electromyography/nerve conduction studies may help differentiate idiopathic toe walking from
toe walking secondary to certain neuromuscular disorders and peripheral neuropathies.
Diagnosis
Idiopathic toe walking is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Differential Diagnosis
Important to rule out other causes, including the following:
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
6/32

Congenital short Achilles tendon
Cerebral palsy
Muscular dystrophy
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Spinal cord or brain injury
Tethered spinal cord
Spina bifida
Autism spectrum disorder
Schizophrenia
Limb-length discrepancy
Clubfoot
Tendon contracture
Ankylosing spondylitis
Unilateral hip dislocation
Plantar foot injuries
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment methods are most successful in children with dorsiflexion beyond 0°.

Nonsurgical Management
Verbal cueing is not effective. Physical therapy and home stretching also are not
effective; however, they often are suggested to help maintain flexibility. Ankle-foot
orthoses (AFO) and rigid shoe inserts are associated with variable results. A randomized
trial that compared cast immobilization and gastrocnemius-soleus complex Botox
injections and revealed a 5° increase in ankle dorsiflexion in both groups, with most
children still intermittently toe walking after treatment.4
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
7/32

Children younger than 5 years with dorsiflexion beyond neutral should be treated via
observation.
Children older than 5 years with less than 10° of dorsiflexion can continue to be observed or
undergo cast immobilization in maximal dorsiflexion for 6 weeks.
If limited dorsiflexion is present, patients can undergo serial cast immobilization in maximal
dorsiflexion every 1 to 2 weeks until sufficient dorsiflexion is achieved.
Techniques/Procedures
Brace management and/or cast immobilization may be attempted in children older than 2
years with dorsiflexion beyond 0°.
Surgical Management
Indications
In children in whom cast immobilization fails or children who have severely limited motion that
cannot achieve neutral ankle dorsiflexion, surgical lengthening may be considered.
May consider an AFO after surgical lengthening if the child continues to toe walk
Techniques/Procedures

Techniques/Procedures
Children older than 2 years with a fixed equinus contracture are candidates for tendon
lengthening. Patients with a fixed contracture in knee flexion/extension should undergo
lengthening of the entire gastrocnemius-soleus complex (Achilles tendon lengthening),
whereas patients with contracture that resolves with knee flexion can undergo recession
of the gastrocnemius alone.
Preoperative Planning
A preoperative Silfverskiöld test is critical to determine if the contracture is isolated to the
gastrocnemius or a combined gastrocnemius-soleus complex contracture.
Patient Positioning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
8/32

Supine or prone, depending on surgeon preference and technique
Surgical Approaches
Always consider the course of the sural nerve, which must be protected.5 (Figure 3; Resource
3)
Isolated gastrocnemius contracture typically is managed via proximal recession, such as a
Baumann or Strayer procedure.
Combined contracture typically is managed via more distal Achilles tendon lengthening, which
may be performed percutaneously (Hoke) or in an open fashion (Z lengthening).
Figure 3 Illustrations show surgical gastric-soleus-Achilles complex lengthening. Zone 1
procedures (ie, Baumann and Strayer) lengthen only the gastrocnemius muscle proximally. Zone
2 procedures (ie, Vulpius and Baker) lengthen the gastrocnemius muscle at its distal tendinous
portion. Zone 3 procedures (ie, White and Hoke) lengthen the Achilles tendon. TAL = Achilles
tendon lengthening. (Reproduced with permission from Ruzbarsky JJ, Scher D, Dodwell E: Toe
walking: Causes, epidemiology, assessment, and treatment. Curr Opin Pediatr 2016;28[1]:40-46.)

Surgical Approaches
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
9/32

For open Z lengthening, a longitudinal incision is made at the midline or medial border
of the Achilles tendon. Next, paratenon flaps are raised in line with the incision. A full-
thickness incision is then made into the midline of the Achilles tendon and exits medial
proximally and lateral distally to avoid the course of the sural nerve. Dorsiflex the ankle
to the desired tension, and secure the limbs of the Achilles tendon back to itself with the
surgeons preferred suture, making sure to avoid prominent knots beneath the skin.
Close the paratenon and then the skin layers.
Postoperative Management
Cast immobilization in desired dorsiflexion in a short leg cast for 6 weeks postoperatively.
May need to transition to an AFO for severe cases
Complications
Achilles rupture/overlengthening
Wound dehiscence
Sural nerve injury
Scar adhesions to the skin
Lengthening will cause a slight weakness to the gastrocnemius-soleus complex.
Higher rate of recurrence with autism spectrum disorder after surgical lengthening
Outcomes
Long-term outcomes of surgical management appear to be more effective than observation or
cast immobilization; however, direct comparison is difficult because of the variability in patient
age and disease severity.
Köhler Disease
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Köhler disease is a self-limiting, painful osteochondrosis of the navicular in young children.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
10/32

Epidemiology
Occurs more commonly in boys than in girls (4:1 ratio)
Usually unilateral
Commonly affects children aged 5 to 6 years
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The navicular is the last tarsal bone to ossify; therefore, it is more susceptible to direct
mechanical compression injury.
Some hypothesize that repetitive mechanical loading occludes the feeding vessels, resulting in
osteonecrosis. A rich perichondral ring of vessels surround the bone, allowing for rapid and
complete revascularization.
Etiology
Unknown; however, histologic studies have found changes in enchondral ossification and bony
ischemia of the ossific nucleus similar to those associated with Perthes disease.
Natural History
Usually unilateral and affects children approximately age 5 or 6 years.
Clinical and radiographic outcomes are excellent in all patients, with no recorded children with
persistent clinical or radiographic abnormalities into adulthood. Irregular ossification of the
navicular is common during early ossification and may be confused with Köhler disease.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Children with Köhler disease typically walk with an antalgic gait and bear weight on the lateral
border of the foot.
Patient History
Midfoot pain
Limp
Warmth (less common)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
11/32

Swelling (less common)
Physical Examination
Tenderness to palpation of the navicular
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs confirm the diagnosis, with flattening, sclerosis, and fragmentation of the
navicular (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Lateral radiograph of the foot of a child with Köhler bone disease demonstrates
sclerosis and flattening of the navicular bone. (Reproduced from Olney BW: Conditions of the
foot, in Abel MF, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Pediatrics, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2006, p 239.)
Köhler disease is diagnosed based on a combination of a symptomatic navicular with the
radiographic findings of flattening, sclerosis, and fragmentation of the navicular.
Asymptomatic children with these radiographic findings do not have Köhler disease6
(Resource 4).
Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
12/32

Symptoms resolve spontaneously within 6 to 15 months.
The navicular reconstitutes in 6 to 48 months.
No residual deformity or disability occurs in adulthood.
Nonsurgical Management
Cast immobilization in a short leg walking cast for 4 to 8 weeks will decrease the duration of
symptoms.
Surgical management is never indicated.
Tarsal Coalition
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The cause of symptoms is not precisely known but may be related to the transition of a
cartilaginous coalition to bone during late childhood and early adolescence.
Overview
An osseous, cartilaginous, or fibrous connection between the tarsal bones

Overview
Coalitions tend to occur in 1% to 6% of the population. Of patients with a tarsal coalition,
10% to 20% have multiple coalitions, and 50% are bilateral. Calcaneonavicular coalitions
are the most common type and occur in children aged 8 to 12 years. Talocalcaneal
coalitions are the second most common type, occurring in children aged 12 to 15 years.
They can occur at any of the three facets of the subtalar joint, with the middle facet
being the most common.
Epidemiology
Autosomal dominant with high penetrance
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
13/32

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
May involve a bony, fibrous, or cartilaginous bar between any of the tarsal bones; most
commonly calcaneonavicular or talocalcaneal (usually middle facet).
Natural History
May be asymptomatic
Risk Factors
May be associated with the following:
Fibular hemimelia
Proximal focal femoral deficiency
Symphalangism
Carpal coalition
Apert syndrome
Ball-and-socket ankle joint
Classification
CT based classification system
Calcaneonavicular coalition7
Type I: cortical irregularities at tip of calcaneus or ossicles between the calcaneus or
navicular bones
Type II: fibrous
Type III: cartilaginous fusion with distinct squaring off of the cuboid
Type IV: complete osseous fusion
Talocalcaneal coalition8 (Figure 5)
Type I: linear
Type II: linear with posterior hook
Type III: shingled
Type IV: complete osseous
Type V: posterior
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
14/32

Figure 5 Coronal CT scans (left) and three-dimensional CT reconstruction images (right)
show the classification of talocalcaneal coalitions. (Reproduced with permission from
Rozansky A, Varley E, Moor M, Wenger DR, Mubarak SJ: A radiologic classification of
talocalcaneal coalitions based on 3D reconstruction. J Child Orthop 2010;4[2]:129-135.).
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The patient may report a history of frequent ankle sprains.
Classic presentation is in a young teenager.
Instability of gait on uneven terrain
Physical Examination
The hallmark physical examination finding is absent or restricted passive subtalar motion.

Physical Examination
The patient may present with a symptomatic rigid pes planovalgus deformity. Standing
physical examination from behind may reveal a fixed hindfoot valgus during toe rise.
Hindfoot motion usually is limited on physical examination. A double medial malleolus
sign may be present in patients with a talocalcaneal coalition9,10 (Figure 6 and Figure 7).

Radiographs should include weight-bearing AP, lateral, internal oblique, and Harris views
(Table 2; Figure 8).


Radiography
Lateral radiographs may demonstrate dorsal talar beaking of the calcaneus, which is a
nonspecific finding associated with many coalitions. This is not a sign of degenerative
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
18/32

arthrosis. Lateral and oblique foot radiographs also may demonstrate the anteater nose
sign, which is an extension of the dorsal aspect of the anterior process of the calcaneus
toward the navicular. This is indicative of a calcaneonavicular collation.
A C-sign is continuity of the posterior aspect of the talus with the sustentaculum tail. This
sign should increase suspicion for a talocalcaneal coalition if clinically indicated. Harris
axial radiographs are associated with a high false-positive rate for talocalcaneal coalition.
If the view is slightly oblique to the posterior or middle facet, a coalition will appear to be
present but it is not.
Computed Tomography
CT is necessary to delineate the coalition and clarify whether a child has multiple coalitions in
the foot. CT also is helpful in surgical planning.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may help identify a fibrous coalition if high suspicion remains and CT scans are
unrevealing.
Diagnosis
Clinical suspicion, radiographs, and advanced imaging studies are used to confirm the
diagnosis.
Differential Diagnosis
Ankle sprain
Painful flatfoot
Spastic peroneal flatfoot or other neurologic condition
Management
Asymptomatic coalitions may be observed.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
19/32

Nonsurgical Management
Initial management of symptomatic patients includes
NSAIDs
Activity modifications
Accommodative shoe orthoses
Immobilization.
Subtalar injection may be helpful in patients with a talocalcaneal coalition.
Some surgeons recommend a short leg walking cast for 2 to 4 weeks followed by a University
of California–Berkeley Lab orthosis.11 With this algorithm, Braddock12 had the following
outcomes in 28 patients followed for a mean of 12 years: 50% had resolution of pain, 40% had
continued mild pain, and 10% had disabling pain warranting surgical management.
Surgical Management
Calcaneonavicular coalition
Coalition resection with or without interposition of the extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) or
autogenous fat is effective in most patients.
Contraindications to resection are advanced degenerative changes in adjacent joints or
multiple coalitions.
Talocalcaneal coalition
Resection traditionally has been limited to small coalitions (middle facet coalition size <50%
the width of the posterior facet) with minimal hindfoot valgus (<20°) and no degenerative
arthrosis. More recent studies have questioned these recommendations.

Surgical Management
If severe valgus is present at the time of coalition excision, calcaneal osteotomy via
lateral column lengthening (such as an Evans osteotomy) or a medial heel slide improves
the clinical outcome and reduces the risk of recurrent symptoms. Osteotomies of the
calcaneal tuberosity, cuboid, and medial cuneiform (triple C osteotomies) have been
used to correct a rigid flatfoot deformity without resection of the coalition. Subtalar
arthrodesis may be indicated in patients with a large talocalcaneal coalition, if
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
20/32

degenerative arthrosis is present, or if coalition resection fails to relieve symptoms.
Triple arthrodesis may be indicated if multiple coalitions are present.
Indications
Disabling pain despite prolonged nonsurgical management
Techniques/Procedures
Patient Positioning
Supine
Surgical Approaches
Calcaneonavicular coalition resection

Calcaneonavicular coalition resection
Classically, an oblique (Ollier) incision along Langer lines is made directly over the
coalition just dorsal to the dorsum of the anterior calcaneal process. Alternatively, an
extensible longitudinal incision may be centered over the coalition. The superficial
peroneal nerve branches are avoided. The EDB is released proximally and elevated from
proximal to distal to expose the coalition. Approximately 1 cm of coalition is resected.
Bone wax can be used to cover the exposed cancellous bone of the talus and calcaneus,
and an autologous fat graft or EDB muscle belly can be used as an interposition to avoid
bony regrowth. The EDB, if used, is held in place by passing sutures through the plantar
medial aspect of the foot, which are then secured to a button outside the skin with
gentle tension.
Talocalcaneal coalition resection
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
21/32


Talocalcaneal coalition resection
A longitudinal medial incision is made 1 cm distal to the medial malleolus between the
posterior tibial tendon and the flexor digitorum longus. The posterior tibial tendon
sheath is identified and incised, and the tendon is retracted dorsally while the flexor
digitorum longus is released from its sheath and retracted plantarly. The deep posterior
tibial tendon sheath and the periosteum are then incised, exposing the middle facet
coalition. Osteotomes, curets, and burrs may be used until visualization of the posterior
facet is possible and motion of the subtalar joint is allowed. Bone wax is used to cover
the exposed cancellous bone, and autologous fat graft is interposed at the resection site
to prevent regrowth.
Postoperative Management
For a calcaneonavicular coalition and middle facet talocalcaneal resection, immobilization in a
splint for 2 weeks postoperatively followed by active ankle and subtalar range of motion with
non–weight-bearing for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Incomplete resection is not uncommon, particularly plantarly during removal of a
calcaneonavicular coalition.
Three-dimensional CT reconstruction images are helpful preoperatively. The subtypes of the
coalitions must be understood preoperatively.
Advanced preoperative imaging studies are mandatory. Even if a coalition is easily identified
on plain radiograph, CT scans must be obtained to assess for a second ipsilateral coalition.
In patients with pain and a rigid flatfoot deformity, surgeons should not assume that coalition
excision alone will be successful. Surgeons should assess for pain from the coalition and the
flatfoot deformity and be prepared to address both in a single (talocalcaneal coalition) or
staged (calcaneonavicular coalition) fashion.
Complications
Wound dehiscence from fat autograft site
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Foot Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004062
22/32

Nerve pain or numbness from injury to the superficial peroneal nerve branches during the
approach to a calcaneonavicular coalition
Regrowth of the coalition
Continued pain, stiffness, deformity (pes planovalgus)
Continued pain may warrant repeat CT to reassess the coalition for recurrence or incomplete
removal.
Outcomes
Calcaneonavicular coalition resection outcomes generally are good, with more than 80% of
patients reporting good pain relief.

Outcomes
Mahan et al13 studied 20 patients with a talocalcaneal coalition and 43 patients with
calcaneonavicular coalition at a mean of 4 years after surgical excision. Both groups had
similar modified American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society ankle-hindfoot scores
and University of California–Los Angeles activity scores at follow-up, which were
indicative of good or excellent function. The authors concluded that more than 70% of
patient activities were not limited by pain and the patients’ functional outcomes were
excellent. They also found that the type of coalition did not seem to be a predictive
factor in determining outcomes.
Toe Disorders
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Atavistic great toe
Abduction deformity of the great toe that usually presents after walking age
Thought to be secondary to an imbalance between the great toe abductor and the adductor
musculature
Typically resolves with age
Resistant cases may require release of the abductor hallucis longus muscle.
SEND FEEDBACK

Polydactyly
Toe polydactyly occurs in 1 in 500 births.
Postaxial polydactyly is most common.
Postaxial polydactyly most often is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
Surgical management is indicated to facilitate shoe wear and prevent toe deformities14
(Figure 10).
Figure 10 Clinical photograph of the foot of an 18-month-old patient shows a rudimentary
sixth toe. (Reproduced with permission from Herring JA: Disorders of the foot, in Tachdjian’s
Pediatric Orthopaedics: From the Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for Children, ed 6. Philadelphia, PA,
Elsevier, 2020.)
Syndactyly
Occurs in approximately 1 in 2,000 births and often is familial
Characterized as simple (fusion of soft tissues) or complex (fusion of bones)
Most frequently occurs between the second and third toes followed by webbing between the
third and fourth toes
Simple syndactyly is an aesthetic deformity that rarely requires surgical management.
Overlapping fifth toe
A dorsal adduction deformity of the fifth toe that overlaps the fourth toe
It typically is familial and bilateral.
The extensor digitorum longus tendon is contracted.

Curly toes
Malrotation and flexion deformity of one or more toes
Contracture of the flexor digitorum longus or the flexor digitorum brevis is the most
common cause.
Management involves flexor tendon tenotomy if not resolved by age 4 to 6 years16 (Figure

Polydactyly
Postaxial polydactyly is duplication of the fifth toe and is most common.
Preaxial polydactyly is duplication of the great toe.
Curly toes
Flexion and medial deviation of the proximal interphalangeal joint
Etiology
Atavistic great toe
May be congenital or acquired
Polydactyly
30% of patients with postaxial polydactyly have a positive family history.
Postaxial polydactyly typically is autosomal dominant.
Hox genes have been identified as loci.
Abnormalities in the BMP4 gene may cause preaxial and postaxial polydactyly.
Curly toes
In general, patients have a positive family history, and the disorder is autosomal dominant.
Overlapping fifth toe
Present at birth and thought to be genetic
Natural History
Curly toes
Resolution in 24% of patients with persistence in the remaining patients
Risk Factors
Polydactyly
Trisomy 13
Ellis-Van Creveld syndrome
Tibial hemimelia
Down syndrome
Approximately 30% of children with polydactyly of the foot will have polydactyly of the hand.
Syndactyly
Observed in patients with Apert syndrome

Classification
Atavistic great toe
First type is from the taut fibrous band between the first metatarsal and the great toe
medially.
Second type can occur from longitudinal bracket epiphysis or preaxial polydactyly.
Third type is part of an underlying skeletal dysplasia, such as diastrophic dwarfism.
Polydactyly
Type A is a well-formed articulated digit.
Type B is a rudimentary digit.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Atavistic great toe
Patients report difficulty with shoe wear or cosmetic concerns.
Deformity may worsen with age.
Overlapping fifth toe
Pain over the dorsum of the fifth toe because of local irritation from wearing shoes
Usually bilateral
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Overlapping fifth toe
Buddy taping is not effective.
Curly toes
Can tape, which will improve toe position transiently; however, deformity generally returns.
Surgical Management
Atavistic great toe
Release of the tight tissues on the medial side of the toe including the abductor hallucis and
medial metatarsophalangeal (MTP) capsule

Syndactyly
Purely cosmetic and requires counseling the patient that no treatment generally is better

Overlapping fifth toe
Management is surgical and involves release of the contracted extensor tendon, dorsal
capsulotomy of the MTP joint, and excision of the abnormal skin crease between the fourth
and fifth toes.
Curly toes
Surgical management recommended for children with persistent deformity at age 6 years
Outcomes similar to those of flexor tenotomy versus flexor-to-extensor transfer

Surgical Management
Atavistic great toe
The great toe often is syndactylized to the second toe to maintain the correction.
Temporary Kirschner wire fixation across the MTP joint often is used to allow the
surrounding tissue to heal. Arthrodesis is reserved for refractory or arthritic cases.
Polydactyly
The goal is to improve cosmesis and shoe fitting. In general, the outer duplicated toes
are amputated unless they are more developed than the inner toe. If inner toes are
removed, surgeons must repair the capsule and the intermetatarsal ligament.
Syndactyly
Apert syndrome syndactyly should not be managed surgically. Syndactyly may occur in
combination with polydactyly. In these patients, the skin from the amputated toe should
be preserved in flaps for closure of the salvaged toe.
Overlapping fifth toe
Dorsal incisions should be avoided to prevent risk of recurrence. Temporary fixation with
the use of a Kirschner wire often is helpful. The Butler procedure commonly is

Preoperative Planning
Polydactyly
Preoperative radiographs should be obtained to define the bony anatomy of the duplication
and identify the structures that should be excised.
Complications
Hallux varus is a common complication of preaxial polydactyly if the soft tissues are not
perfectly balanced after removal of the supernumerary digit.
